SidLens: mechanistic analysis of SID recommenders

Qwen-AR and DiffGRM on Amazon Industrial & Scientific (3,105 items) · review copy built 2026-10-18 · 15 AR, 10 diffusion and 2 SID-map experiments

On this pageOpening questionsRecommended claimsOrder of the write-upContext-only experimentsNext steps
Provisional results. Every number on this page comes from the checkpoints we have now: two AR next-item models, one AR next-two model, 12 retrained AR models and 20 DiffGRM models. The paper's final numbers will come from rerunning the full analysis on the intermediate checkpoints of the final training run (with our co-author). We expect the trends to hold, but we have not checked that yet, so treat the values here as a preview of the write-up, not as its final results.

Storyline and recommendations

This tab proposes how to organize the write-up. It lists the questions to open with, the claims we recommend making, and for each claim the experiments that support it and the experiments that set it up. Every experiment on the other tabs appears here at least once. Click an experiment to open it.

Opening questions

  1. RQ1 · Maps. How do RQ-KMeans, RQ-VAE and MQ assign items to SID digits, and why do different items end up with the same SID?
  2. RQ2 · Representation. What does each layer of an AR and a masked-diffusion recommender hold about the final recommendation, and when does information from the history become the answer?
  3. RQ3 · Computation. Which history information produces each digit, through which parts of the network, and how do the AR and diffusion recommenders differ across maps?
  4. RQ4 · From scores to reported results. How do decoding and evaluation turn digit scores into reported accuracy, and which hits come from items the history already identifies?

Recommended claims

RQ1 · claim 1

SID maps differ in what a digit means, and post-processing decides most collisions.

In RQ-KMeans and RQ-VAE, digit 1 alone explains 34–53 % of the embedding variance and later digits 8–18 %; MQ's four digits explain 36–38 % each. RQ-VAE's near-zero collision rate comes from a last-digit reassignment; the same step removes nearly all RQ-KMeans collisions.

RQ2 · claim 2

Neither model holds information about new targets beyond the history; what is readable is the item to copy.

AR: the target's first digit is never probed above 'predict the recent item's first digit'; the copy appears in the output from layer 20. DiffGRM: the encoder output predicts new targets no better than its input (±0.011), while the recent item becomes readable from every slot.

RQ3 · claim 3

Both recommenders copy each digit from a history item that matches the prefix written so far.

AR: changing a matching history item costs 1.35 / 1.06 nats, a non-matching one about 0; this holds in all 12 retrained AR models. DiffGRM: 0.35 / 0.96 vs about 0. Both rely most on the most recent item (0.57 / 0.51 nats AR, 0.56 / 0.48 DiffGRM).

RQ3 · claim 4

The two paradigms copy through different routes.

AR reads the matching item's digit token directly, by attention in layers 14–27, spread over many heads (top 5 heads: 8–9 %). DiffGRM's encoder spreads the recent item into the other slots: their clean states restore 0.83–0.90 of a replaced item's effect against 0.32–0.53 for its own slot, and each decoder digit reads the history through its own cross-attention.

RQ3 · claim 5

DiffGRM decides most of the SID at the first reveal step, and digits exchange information in the first decoder block.

Switching the history at the first step alone gives the swapped-history result for 16–68 % of affected users (more at width 512 in 9 of 9 pairs), at the last step for 1–10 %. A revealed digit's effect reaches the predicted digit after block 1 (0.65–0.96 restored), mostly over the direct edge (0.37–0.89, lower at depth 5).

RQ3 · claim 6

Neither model uses time. AR follows list position; DiffGRM follows the item but reads absolute slot positions.

In the data, the recent item predicts the target mainly on the same day. RQ-KMeans AR copies it whatever its age and prefers whichever item is last (position effect 0.36–0.39). After a swap, DiffGRM keeps copying the same item (0–18 % follow the slot), but moving the history five slots changes its top-1 for 47–82 % of users.

RQ3 · claim 7

In next-two prediction, the second item is copied from the first.

Replacing item 1 costs item 2's first digit 0.60 nats, against 0.20 for the most recent history item; copying between the two predicted items costs 0.43–0.73 nats in matching rows.

RQ4 · claim 8

Search settings change the reported comparison of reveal orders.

At beam 64, confidence order loses 0.95 pp of HR@10 to fixed order (2.6 pp at depth 5); at beam 256 it wins by 0.22 pp. Duplicate paths fill 57–91 % of the confidence beam. The best fixed order differs by quantizer.

RQ4 · claim 9

Copying raises hit rates only on items the user already had, and SID-level metrics overstate the gain.

Blocking copying in beam search costs AR 27 / 10 pp on repeat targets and DiffGRM 12–39 pp, and about 0 on truly new items. In AR, collision partners and near-duplicate variants carry 56 % and 80 % of the loss, and only 28 % of RQ-KMeans' top-rank benefit remains at item level. SID HR@10 exceeds item HR@10 by 4.5 pp.

Order of the write-up

  1. Opening. State the four questions. Explain SIDs, the two paradigms, and that we compare what they compute on shared maps, not their scores.
  2. RQ1 · Maps. Structure exp1, exp2 and semantic mapping, then Structure exp3.
  3. RQ2 · Representation. Representation exp1 → Representation exp2 → Representation exp3 for AR; Representation exp5 and Representation exp4 for DiffGRM.
  4. RQ3 · Computation. Retrospective exp2 (motivation) → Controlled exp3 → Controlled exp4 → Controlled exp10 → Controlled exp11; then Controlled exp7 → Controlled exp8 → Controlled exp12 → Controlled exp13; then Controlled exp9, Retrospective exp6 and the swap/shift part of Controlled exp14; next-two (Controlled exp5) last.
  5. RQ4 · Scores to results. Retrospective exp1 → Controlled exp1 → Controlled exp2 for search; then Controlled exp6 → Retrospective exp7 → Retrospective exp3 and the copy-block part of Controlled exp14 for what the hits measure.
  6. Limits. One checkpoint per map; provisional numbers until the final-run checkpoints are analysed; different AR and DiffGRM cohorts.

Experiments that serve as context only

  • Retrospective exp4: Next-two association in archived lists An association in saved lists; exp5 is the causal test. Appendix.
  • Retrospective exp1: Confidence vs fixed reveal order in the archived runs Archived runs with unequal beams; it motivates exp1 and exp2 but tests nothing on its own.
  • Retrospective exp3: Collisions and SID-level accuracy Supports the item-credit claim; one sentence and a table may be enough.
  • Controlled exp10: The last digit: copy it or avoid it Shows how map post-processing changes copying of the last digit. RQ-VAE's declared estimate includes 0, so it fits a discussion paragraph better than a main claim.

Final important experiments

This tab proposes the experiments to run on the checkpoints of the final training run, for review before we build the pipeline. They fall into three lines: codebooks and collisions (M), Qwen-AR (AR) and DiffGRM (DG). Each line lists its main experiments first and its supplementary experiments after: 13 main and 10 supplementary, plus three shared steps that come first. Every experiment on the other tabs maps to one of them (Coverage). Nothing here has run on the final checkpoints. The "Current result" lines quote the provisional numbers that the final run should confirm or replace.

What the final run contains

We assume the final run is the full grid of the OneDiffRec handoff (run_grid.sh, run name grid-v1, commits up to 16 October 2026). If it turns out narrower, for example only run_next2.sh and run_zcr.sh, the same experiments apply to the configurations that exist.

  • Four blocks: Industrial and Office, each with next-item and next-two prediction.
  • Configurations per block: 27 SID tables refitted from the item embeddings (v3: the RQ-KMeans and RQ-VAE tables of v2, and MQ refitted on 15 October with the coauthors' TokenRec code), each with native SIDs. A table also gets a ZCR model when more than 5 % of its items share a SID, and RQ-VAE 3×256, 4×256 and 5×256 get one by name. build_tables.sh --status gives the exact list. Every configuration has an AR and a DiffGRM model, seed 42.
  • Kept weight states. AR: snapshots at epochs 0.5 and 1.5, and the best model by validation loss (training stops early around epoch 4; the best model is near epoch 2.5 on Industrial). DiffGRM: the best model by validation NDCG, a snapshot every 20 epochs, and the training loss and validation metrics of every epoch.
  • Cohorts: disjoint_horizon_v3. AR and DiffGRM are tested on the same target events, and both see up to 50 history items.
  • Test decoding: exact SIDs, 50 beams for both models. AR uses plain beam search. DiffGRM reveals digits in a fixed left-to-right order and keeps only codes that some catalog SID allows at each step (joint_catalog_v1); a next-two DiffGRM model decodes both items in one pass. Each run saves its ranked predictions, scores, collision strata and item-level (CCE) metrics.

What this changes for the analysis

  1. The SID tables are new. Every map result is recomputed (line M). Results tied to the old tables, such as the balanced RQ-KMeans 5×512 table and the old MQ fit, may not carry over.
  2. AR and DiffGRM are tested on the same events. Their estimates can be compared user by user with paired intervals. With the old cohorts we could only set them side by side.
  3. ZCR twins come from the same pipeline. Each ZCR model has a native twin trained the same way, so M3 and AR4 can test what collisions cause.
  4. Office is a second catalog. Category statistics and title-based variant detection need Office metadata, which we have not downloaded. The other measures need only the embeddings and the run outputs.
  5. Weight states along training. The cheap teacher-forced experiments can run at every kept state: three states per AR run and one every 20 epochs per DiffGRM run.
  6. Our code must read the v3 inputs first. That means v3 AR prompts with 50 history items, v3 cohorts, two-item DiffGRM checkpoints and the v3 DiffGRM decoder. The reproduction check becomes: our decoder reproduces each run's saved test predictions.
  7. DiffGRM's test decoder changed. v3 reveals digits left to right and checks legality at every step. Our earlier search results (duplicate paths under confidence order, illegal SIDs under fixed orders) describe the old decoder. DG5 compares the two decoders on the same checkpoints.

Terms used below

Every configuration
All 27 native tables of a block and every ZCR twin.
Focal set
RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 and MQ 3×128, with their ZCR twins where they exist. The first two are the maps of all our earlier work, so their final numbers can be set beside the provisional ones.
Every kept state / best state
All weight states listed above, or only the model the run selected.
User sample
A fixed set of test users per catalog and task (2,000 proposed), drawn once with a recorded seed and shared by both paradigms and all weight states. The full cohort is every test user.

Register, load and check the final run

Can we load every model exactly and reproduce what the run reported?

Hash and register every kept weight state, SID table and ZCR codebook. Make the loaders read v3 prompts, v3 cohorts, two-item DiffGRM checkpoints and the v3 DiffGRM decoder. Reproduce each best state's saved test predictions with our scoring and decoding code. Draw the user samples.

No result may use a model whose predictions we cannot reproduce. This check replaces the archive check of the earlier experiments.

Line M: codebooks and collisions

These experiments read the SID tables, the ZCR codebooks, the item embeddings and the labels. M3 and M4 also read each run's saved predictions. None of them needs model weights.

Main experiments

M1 Main

What each digit encodes

Question
How does each quantizer split items into digits?
Measures
For each table: the share of embedding variance explained by each digit alone and given its prefix; the codes in use per digit; the category information each digit adds given the prefix, against a null that shuffles items within each parent; category purity by prefix length, against a shuffled null.
Checks
Nulls keep group sizes.
Runs on
All 54 native tables and every ZCR codebook. Category measures on Industrial until Office metadata is downloaded.
Cost
CPU, hours.
Builds on
Structure exp1, exp2 and semantic mapping: What each SID digit encodes
What is new
Refitted tables; a new MQ fit.
Current result
In the 4×128 tables, digit 1 alone explains 53 % (RQ-KMeans) and 34 % (RQ-VAE) of the variance and each later digit 8–18 %; each MQ digit explains 36–38 %. Category purity stops rising after digit 3. RQ-VAE uses 2–31 % of its digit-1 codes in 8 of 9 fits.
In the paper
The per-digit information figure (RQ1).
M2 Main

Why items share a SID

Question
What makes distinct items end up with the same SID in each family?
Measures
The share of items whose SID is shared; how many of those have identical or near-identical embeddings; the rate before and after RQ-VAE's last-digit reassignment, applied to every table; items on a near-origin code at each level; redundancy between MQ digits (NMI against an independent-digit null).
Checks
Refit each RQ-KMeans table and confirm it reproduces (the fit depends on the FAISS thread count).
Runs on
All 54 native tables.
Cost
CPU, about a day with refits.
Builds on
Structure exp3: Why items share a SID
What is new
v3 RQ-KMeans tables are unbalanced FAISS fits, so the old 5×512 balancing result does not apply.
Current result
RQ-VAE's near-zero rates come from the reassignment, which takes RQ-KMeans tables from 10–45 % to the 22 items with identical inputs. Near-duplicates are 73–85 % of collided items in the deepest RQ-KMeans fits. MQ digits repeat each other (NMI 0.50–0.70).
In the paper
The collision-cause table (RQ1).

Line AR: Qwen-AR

RQ2–RQ4

These experiments load AR weights. AR1 is the only AR experiment proposed for every kept state; the others run on the best state.

Main experiments

AR1 Main

History use and prefix-matched copying, along training

Question
How much does each digit depend on the most recent history item and on history items that match the prefix written so far, and when during training does this appear?
Measures
Under teacher forcing: the cost to the true digit-1 code of replacing the history item at recency r (A1, r up to 50); the share left when the replacement keeps the item's first m digits (A3); changing digit d of a history item that matches the target on the earlier digits, minus the same change on a non-matching item (H1); knocking out the attention edge from digit d's readout to the matching item's digit-d token, minus a control edge (H2b); the share of H2b in the later half of the layers.
Checks
No-op knockouts are bit-exact on every row.
Runs on
Industrial: every next-item configuration at every kept state. Office: every configuration at the best state, the focal set at every state. Test-cohort user sample; the validation cohort as a replication at the best state.
Cost
20–31 GPU-minutes per model and split on the old short prompts; longer with 50 items. The largest cost in the plan.
Builds on
Controlled exp3: Replacing one history item, and where its information goesControlled exp4: Prefix-matched copying and the attention edge that carries itControlled exp11: Copying across 12 retrained AR models
What is new
50-item histories; ZCR twins; weight states; the same users as DG1.
Current result
In all 12 retrained models: A1 0.37–0.78 nats, H1 0.89–2.18, H2b 0.20–0.60, and 98–100 % of the edge effect in layers 14–27.
In the paper
The history and copying table and the grid figure (RQ3); a training panel if the states differ.
AR2 Main

What copying buys in beam search

Question
Which hits depend on copying?
Measures
During the v3 beam search, when a beam predicts digit d, block its reads of digit d of every history item whose earlier digits equal the beam's own prefix (at digit 1, of every history item), in the later half of the layers. Control: block the same number of non-matching items. Change in Hit@10 by target class (S2), at SID and item level.
Checks
The unblocked search reproduces the run's saved predictions.
Runs on
Every next-item configuration (native and ZCR), both catalogs, best state; Office on the user sample.
Cost
About 10–13 GPU-minutes per decode of 3,681 events on the old prompts; three decodes per model (unblocked, blocked, control).
Builds on
Controlled exp6: Blocking copying inside beam searchRetrospective exp7: Which targets the copy benefit comes fromControlled exp11: Copying across 12 retrained AR models
What is new
Plain 50-beam search is now the reported decoder; the target classes come from S2.
Current result
The copy block costs 7.5–37.0 points of Hit@10 on repeat targets and 0.1–4.3 on new targets (12 models). In RQ-KMeans 3×128, SID partners carry 56 % of the loss, and 28 % of the top-1 benefit remains at item level.
In the paper
The RQ4 copy-benefit figure, beside DG4 on the same events.
AR3 Main

What each layer holds

Question
From which layer can the model's own answer be read, does any layer hold information about new targets beyond the history, and when does the copied item become the answer?
Measures
Activations at the digit readout positions of every layer; logit lens and tuned lens for the model's own answer, the true target and the copy source, per digit; whole-SID decoders; probes for the target on new-target rows against the rule "predict the recent item's digit".
Checks
User-disjoint folds; majority and shuffled-label baselines.
Runs on
Industrial: every native next-item configuration at the best state. The focal set at every kept state and on Office.
Cost
Captures, estimated at about 15 GPU-minutes per model; lenses and probes on CPU.
Builds on
Representation exp1: Layer-by-layer readout of the first digitRepresentation exp3: Information map across all layers
What is new
Readout curves across the grid instead of two models.
Current result
The final first-digit choice equals the recent item's first digit in 64 / 53 % of rows (RQ-KMeans 3×128 / RQ-VAE 4×128). The preference for the copy appears at layers 20–23 in RQ-KMeans and at layers 11 and 20 in RQ-VAE. No layer reads the target above the copy rule.
In the paper
The layer readout figure (RQ2).
AR4 Main

The last digit: copy or avoid, native against ZCR

Question
When a history item matches the target on every digit but the last, does the model copy its last code, and does removing collisions change that?
Measures
Knock out the edge from the last digit's readout to that item's last-digit token, minus a control edge. Change in the item's own code and in the target's code, in rows where the target has that item's SID and in rows where it is a sibling. Native minus ZCR twin.
Checks
No-op knockouts bit-exact.
Runs on
Every native/ZCR pair, next-item, both catalogs, best state.
Cost
Teacher forcing, about as much as AR1 per model.
Builds on
Controlled exp10: The last digit: copy it or avoid it
What is new
The causal test the ZCR runs were commissioned for.
Current result
RQ-KMeans 3×128 copies the last digit (−0.17 / −0.34 nats, test / validation). RQ-VAE 4×128 avoids it in sibling rows: blocking raises top-1 = that item's code by 11.8 points. RQ-VAE's declared pooled estimate includes 0.
In the paper
An RQ3 paragraph; a figure if the twins change consistently.

Supplementary experiments

AR5 Supplementary

Where the recent item's information goes

Question
Through which positions and heads does the history item's information reach the answer?
Measures
Residual-stream patching by layer and position (item tokens, response header, target positions); a screen of attention heads for the copy edge, with held-out users.
Checks
A patch must fire exactly once; no-op patches bit-exact.
Runs on
Focal set, best state.
Cost
GPU, hours per model.
Builds on
Controlled exp3: Replacing one history item, and where its information goesControlled exp4: Prefix-matched copying and the attention edge that carries it
What is new
—
Current result
The item's information stays at its tokens until about layers 16–20 and moves to the header and target positions in layers 19–24; the top 5 heads carry 8–9 % of the edge effect.
In the paper
Appendix, or one sentence in RQ3.
AR6 Supplementary

Sparse features of copying

Question
Which features carry the copy, and are they used?
Measures
TopK SAEs on the residual stream at every second layer; a census of what each feature tracks; error-preserving ablation of copy features and prefix-match features at the readout, against control features.
Checks
Reconstruction error and splice tests before any ablation counts.
Runs on
Focal set, best state; epoch 1.5 as well if AR1 shows copying changes between states.
Cost
Heavy: training-split captures and SAE training.
Builds on
Representation exp2: Sparse autoencoders on the AR residual streamRepresentation exp3: Information map across all layers
What is new
—
Current result
Copy features are causal from layer 20 (0.10–0.36 nats); RQ-KMeans' sharp prefix-match features have no effect at the readout.
In the paper
Appendix; one RQ2 sentence.
AR7 Supplementary

Order and time

Question
Does the model follow list position or review time?
Measures
Swap the two most recent history items, split by whether they share a review day (S2); the rate at which the model copies the recent item's first digit, by the item's age, against the same rate in the data.
Checks
Swaps of items with identical SIDs are bit-exact.
Runs on
Every native next-item configuration, best state, user sample.
Cost
Teacher forcing, below AR1.
Builds on
Controlled exp9: Order versus time: swapping the two most recent itemsRetrospective exp6: Time in the data and in the models' copying
What is new
50-item histories; repeat without copied-review pairs (S2).
Current result
RQ-KMeans 3×128 follows position (position effect 0.36–0.38), RQ-VAE 4×128 weakly (0.07–0.10); a swap that keeps the review days flips 50 % of first-digit choices.
In the paper
Appendix.
AR8 Supplementary

Next-two: item 2 from item 1

Question
Is the second predicted item copied from the first?
Measures
Replace item 1 or the most recent history item and measure item 2's digits; prefix-matched copying from item 1 to item 2; patching item 1's tokens (focal set); exact ordered-pair hits from the saved lists.
Checks
No-op controls bit-exact.
Runs on
Every next-two configuration, both catalogs, best state, user sample; the focal set at every kept state.
Cost
Teacher forcing, about AR1 per model.
Builds on
Controlled exp5: Next-two prediction: item 2 is copied from item 1Retrospective exp4: Next-two association in archived lists
What is new
The grid instead of one model.
Current result
Replacing item 1 costs item 2's first digit 0.60 nats, against 0.20 for the most recent history item (one model, MQ 4×256).
In the paper
A short RQ3 subsection, beside DG9.
AR9 Supplementary

Where the answer first goes wrong

Question
At which digit do wrong predictions first leave the target?
Measures
The first digit at which each saved top-1 prediction differs from the target.
Checks
—
Runs on
Every run of both paradigms, saved predictions.
Cost
CPU, minutes.
Builds on
Retrospective exp2: Where AR predictions first go wrong
What is new
DiffGRM gets the same count.

In 82 % of archived AR rows, the top-1 prediction first differs from the target at digit 1.

Line DG: DiffGRM

RQ2–RQ4

DiffGRM experiments cost minutes per model, so most of them can run on every configuration. DG1 and the blocks of DG2 run at every kept state.

Main experiments

DG1 Main

History use and prefix-matched copying, along training

Question
Does DiffGRM depend on the most recent item and copy from prefix-matching items as AR does, and when does this appear?
Measures
The cost to the true digit-1 code of replacing the item at recency r; changing a matching against a non-matching history item (H1); knocking out the decoder's direct cross-attention read of the matching item.
Checks
No-op controls bit-exact.
Runs on
Every next-item configuration (native and ZCR), both catalogs, every kept state, on the same user sample as AR1, so AR minus DiffGRM differences get paired intervals.
Cost
Minutes per weight state.
Builds on
Controlled exp7: What DiffGRM uses from the history
What is new
Weight states; ZCR twins; paired with AR1.
Current result
Replacing the recent item costs 0.56 / 0.48 nats (AR 0.57 / 0.51); copying 0.35 / 0.96 against about 0; the direct read carries almost nothing (−0.007 / −0.004).
In the paper
Beside AR1 in the history and copying table (RQ3).
DG2 Main

Where the copy travels

Question
How does the recent item reach the digit being predicted?
Measures
Block the other slots from reading the recent item in the encoder, block the decoder's direct read, block both, and the same blocks on a control item. Paired runs with the recent item replaced: restore the other slots' encoder states or the item's own slot, and one block's cross-attention output at one digit. Probe the recent item's first code from the other slots.
Checks
Patching every cross-attention output reproduces the donor run; no-op controls bit-exact.
Runs on
Every next-item configuration at the best state; the blocks and the restored shares also at every kept state.
Cost
Minutes per model on CPU.
Builds on
Controlled exp8: The copy reaches the decoder through the encoderControlled exp12: Activation patching between paired runsRepresentation exp5: What the encoder holds: probes, SAEs and a description autoencoder
What is new
Weight states: does the encoder spread form before the direct read?
Current result
The other slots restore 0.83–0.90 of the first-digit effect, the item's own slot 0.32–0.53. Blocking both routes costs 0.24 / 0.60 nats, about two thirds of the replacement effect.
In the paper
The DiffGRM route figure (RQ3), beside AR1's edge knockout.
DG3 Main

What each step and block holds, and which step uses the history

Question
When does the answer become readable, and at which reveal step does the history decide it?
Measures
At every reveal step and decoder block: the readout of the model's own answer, the target and the copy source, and the catalog ranking from the partial SID. Step switch: replace the recent item at one step only and count the affected users whose top-1 follows the switched history. Encoder probes for each slot's own code and for the target on new-target rows.
Checks
Switching at no step reproduces the plain decode, and switching at every step the donor decode, bit for bit.
Runs on
Every next-item configuration at the best state, under the v3 decoder and under confidence order; the focal set at every kept state.
Cost
Minutes per model on one GPU.
Builds on
Representation exp4: Reveal trace: what the decode holds at each stepControlled exp13: At which reveal step DiffGRM uses the historyRepresentation exp5: What the encoder holds: probes, SAEs and a description autoencoder
What is new
Under v3's fixed order, step t always reveals digit t, so step and digit effects separate.
Current result
The first step alone gives the switched result for 16–68 % of affected users, the last step for 1–10 %. The encoder output holds no information about new targets beyond the history (±0.011).
In the paper
The DiffGRM readout panels (RQ2) and the step result (RQ3).
DG4 Main

What copying buys in beam search

Question
Which DiffGRM hits depend on copying?
Measures
Hold DG2's double block on the recent item through the whole v3 search (50 beams), against the same block on a control item. Change in Hit@10 by target class (S2), at SID and item level.
Checks
The unblocked search reproduces the run's saved predictions.
Runs on
Every next-item configuration (native and ZCR), both catalogs, best state.
Cost
Minutes per model on one GPU.
Builds on
Controlled exp14: Perturbations held through decoding: copy block, swap and shift
What is new
The v3 decoder; the same events as AR2.
Current result
The block lowers SID Hit@10 by 1.0–3.7 points overall and by 11.5–38.9 on repeat targets; on new targets the change is −0.7 to +0.4 (19 models).
In the paper
Beside AR2 in the RQ4 copy-benefit figure.
DG5 Main

Search: duplicate paths, reveal orders and merging

Question
How much do search settings change DiffGRM's reported score?
Measures
At equal beam sizes (50 and 256): v3's left-to-right decoder with legality checks; confidence order; all six fixed orders at depth 3; confidence order with one path per partial SID (merging, new). The share of duplicate paths and illegal SIDs in the final beam; SID-level and item-level Hit@10.
Checks
Each decoder reproduces its reference first: v3 the saved predictions, confidence order the vendored decoder.
Runs on
Every native next-item configuration, best state, full cohort.
Cost
GPU, several decodes per model.
Builds on
Controlled exp1: Confidence vs fixed order at the same beam sizeControlled exp2: All six fixed orders at depth 3Retrospective exp1: Confidence vs fixed reveal order in the archived runs
What is new
The v3 decoder and merging are new conditions.
Current result
At beam 64, confidence order loses 0.95 points of Hit@10 to a fixed order (2.6 at depth 5); at beam 256 it wins by 0.22. Duplicates fill 57–91 % of the confidence beam.
In the paper
The search figure (RQ4).

DG7 Supplementary

Encoder features

Question
Which encoder features carry the recent item, and can a short description rebuild a slot?
Measures
TopK SAEs on the encoder output, labelled by the attribute each feature tracks; ablating the features that carry the recent item into other slots; the description autoencoder (eight grounded words per slot) and how much of the decoder's behaviour the rebuilt states keep.
Checks
Splice test before ablation; an empty ablation returns the input exactly.
Runs on
Focal set, best state.
Cost
Minutes per model on one GPU.
Builds on

What is new
—

The spread features are causal in 19 of 20 models (up to 0.36 nats); rebuilt states keep 0.39–0.85 of the behaviour.
In the paper
Appendix.
DG8 Supplementary

Order and position

Question
Does DiffGRM follow the item or its slot, and do absolute positions matter?
Measures
Swap the two most recent items; shift the whole history by 1 and 5 slots, once with padding at the start and once by dropping the oldest items so that no padding appears.
Checks
Declare the swap estimand on the scale used in the analysis (the old one was mis-scaled).
Runs on
Every native next-item configuration, best state.
Cost
Minutes per model on one GPU.
Builds on
Controlled exp14: Perturbations held through decoding: copy block, swap and shift
What is new
The shift without padding; a correctly scaled swap estimand.
Current result
After a swap, 39–86 % of users whose top-1 copied the recent item keep its code; a 5-slot shift changes the top-1 for 47–82 % of users.
In the paper
Appendix, beside AR7.
DG9 Supplementary

Next-two in one decode

Question
In a joint next-two decode, is item 2 copied from item 1, as in AR?
Measures
Change item 1's revealed digits and measure item 2's digits; knock out the self-attention edges from item 2's positions to item 1's; replace the most recent history item against clamping item 1.
Checks
No-op controls bit-exact; the v3 decoder reproduces the saved pair predictions.
Runs on
Every next-two configuration, both catalogs, best state, user sample.
Cost
Minutes per model on one GPU.
Builds on
Controlled exp5: Next-two prediction: item 2 is copied from item 1
What is new
New experiment and protocol. Revealed SID tokens carry no item-slot position embedding in this architecture, so the model must tell the items apart by their mask slots.
Current result
None: the old DiffGRM next-two models decode in two passes.
In the paper
Beside AR8.

Experiments along training

The kept weight states let us ask when copying forms during training. AR has three states (epochs 0.5 and 1.5 and the best model), which is enough to see whether copying is present early and how much it grows. DiffGRM has a state every 20 epochs and the validation metrics of every epoch, so we can also ask whether copying strength rises with validation accuracy.

  • Every kept state: AR1 (Industrial), DG1, and the blocks and restored shares of DG2.
  • Focal set only: AR3, DG3 and AR8.
  • Best state only: the decoding experiments (AR2, DG4, DG5), because intermediate states have no saved predictions to check against. DiffGRM decoding is cheap enough to add the focal set's states later.

This could become a short RQ3 subsection if the states differ. If copying is already at full strength by epoch 0.5, it is one sentence.

Cost

Measured on our earlier jobs, one GPU unless noted:

  • AR teacher-forced battery (controlled exp4 on one split plus exp3's replacement part): 20–31 minutes per model for 3,680 rows with histories of at most 10 items.
  • AR beam search with copy blocks (controlled exp6, six decodes of 3,681 events): 62–80 minutes per model.
  • DiffGRM experiments (representation exp5; controlled exp12 on CPU, exp13 and exp14 on an A100): 4–13 minutes per model for 6,297 users.

v3 AR prompts hold up to 50 history items. We guess they cost 3–5 times as much per row; measure it on the first v3 model. A block has up to about 47 configurations (27 native and up to about 20 ZCR twins), so the AR experiments dominate the cost: AR1 at every kept state on both next-item blocks would take a few hundred GPU-hours at the proposed sample size. The scope proposed in AR1 (every state on Industrial, the best state on Office) cuts that by about 30 %. DiffGRM experiments cost minutes per model and can run everywhere.

Decisions for your review

  1. Confirm that the final run is the four-block grid, or tell us which blocks exist.
  2. AR1 scope: every kept state on Industrial and the best state on Office (proposed), or every state on both.
  3. User-sample size (2,000 proposed) and whether the declared estimates use the test cohort (proposed) or the validation cohort.
  4. Focal set: RQ-VAE 4×128 has no ZCR twin if its collision rate stays under 5 %. Add RQ-VAE 4×256, which gets a twin by name?
  5. Download the Office metadata, so that M1, M5 and S2 have categories and titles for Office.
  6. Main DiffGRM decoder: the v3 left-to-right decoder that the runs report (proposed), with confidence order as a condition in DG3 and DG5.
  7. Whether training dynamics becomes a sub-question of RQ3. Decide after AR1 and DG1 on the first block.
  8. If seed replicates are trained, run AR1, DG1, AR2 and DG4 on them to measure training noise.

Provisional results. Every number on this page comes from the checkpoints we have now: two AR next-item models, one AR next-two model, 12 retrained AR models and 20 DiffGRM models. The paper's final numbers will come from rerunning the full analysis on the intermediate checkpoints of the final training run (with our co-author). We expect the trends to hold, but we have not checked that yet, so treat the values here as a preview of the write-up, not as its final results.

AR experiments

The AR recommender is Qwen2.5-1.5B fine-tuned to write a SID digit by digit after a prompt that lists the user's history as SIDs. Two next-item models have weights: RQ-KMeans 3×128 (next-item_best) and RQ-VAE 4×128 (oneoff_rqvae4cb128, a separate run, not the sweep model). One next-two model (MQ 4×256) predicts the next two items, and 12 retrained next-item models cover more maps (exp11). Unless stated, the data are the next-item test split (3,681 events, 1,606 users) under teacher forcing. Effects are given as Δ: how much the target code's log-probability falls (nats). r1 is the most recent history item. Intervals are 95 % user-bootstrap intervals; they do not include training-seed variation.

Retrospective exp2

Where AR predictions first go wrong

18 archived AR next-item configurations (saved lists only) · test split · descriptive, no model run

What we did

For each of the 18 archived AR configurations (widths 128 and 512), we compared every rank-1 prediction with the target digit by digit and recorded the first digit that differs. We also measured how often a digit is right when all earlier digits are right.

Results

Rank-1 exact SID accuracy8.75 % [7.64, 9.85]
Rank-1 digits matched before the first error0.48 of a digit on average
First digit right at rank 117.8 %
SID HR@10 (exact)16.6 %

Takeaways

  • Most rank-1 errors start at the first digit (82 % of rows).
  • When the first digit is right, the later digits are usually right too (64 % at digit 2, 82 % at digit 3).
  • So the first digit is where history matters most, which exp3 tests.

Source: derived/retrospective/exp2_prefix/

Controlled exp3

Replacing one history item, and where its information goes

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · test split, teacher forcing · declared protocol

What we did

We replaced one history item with a catalogue item that shares its first m digits and differs at digit m+1 (m = 0: a different first digit), re-encoded the prompt, and measured the fall in the target code's log-probability at each digit. We did this for each of the 10 most recent items.

To find where the replaced item's information goes, we ran the corrupted prompt and copied the clean run's activations back in at one layer and one group of positions: the item's own tokens, the tokens between it and the answer, the response header, or the target tokens. Recovery is the share of the effect that comes back.

Results

Replace r1, first digit (m = 0)RQ-KMeans 0.57 [0.53, 0.62] · RQ-VAE 0.51 [0.47, 0.55] nats
Top-1 first digit changes in75 % · 50 % of rows
Second most recent item0.16 · 0.22 nats
Effect left when the control keeps r1's first digit18 % · 36 %
Item tokens still hold the effect (recovery ≥ 0.95) throughlayer 20 · layer 16 (of 28)
Response header recovers ≥ 0.5 fromlayer 21 · layer 20

Takeaways

  • Both models rely mostly on the most recent item, and mostly on its first digit.
  • The item's information stays at its own tokens until about layer 20 and then moves to the answer positions in layers 19–24. The tokens in between never carry it.
  • A post-hoc split found that changes to later digits matter almost only when the history item already matches the target's earlier digits. This led to the prefix-matched copying hypothesis, tested in exp4.

Source: derived/controlled/exp3_ar_history_patching/summary-280961/

Controlled exp4

Prefix-matched copying and the attention edge that carries it

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · validation split (3,680 rows); test split as secondary · declared protocol, tested on data not used to form the hypothesis

What we did

We tested the copy hypothesis from exp3 on the validation split. First, we changed digit d onward of the most recent item and compared rows where that item already matches the target's first d digits with rows where it does not. Second, we blocked a single attention edge: from the position that predicts digit d to the matching item's digit-d token, in all layers, in layers 0–13 only, or in layers 14–27 only. Controls block the same edge to a non-matching item. Third, we picked the 5 heads with the largest edge effect on half of the users and tested them on the other half against random heads from the same layers.

Results

Change r1's digits ≥ d, matching rowsRQ-KMeans 1.35 · RQ-VAE 1.06 nats
Same, non-matching rows0.01 · 0.03 nats
Block the one edge to the matching digit-d token0.40 [0.32, 0.48] · 0.36 [0.31, 0.42] nats
Same block in layers 0–13 / layers 14–270.000 / 0.395 · 0.001 / 0.355 nats
Share of the edge effect carried by the top-5 heads9 % · 8 %

Takeaways

  • To choose digit d, both models copy digit d of a history item that matches the prefix they have already written.
  • The copy is a direct attention read of that item's digit-d token, entirely in layers 14–27.
  • Many heads share the read. Five heads carry less than a tenth of it, so there is no small circuit to point to.

Source: derived/controlled/exp4_ar_copy_circuit/summary-281261/

Controlled exp10

The last digit: copy it or avoid it

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · test and validation splits · declared protocol

What we did

We took rows where a history item h matches the target on every digit before the last. We blocked the attention edge from the last digit's prediction position to h's last-digit token (layers 14–27), against a matched control edge. We split rows by whether the target is h's own SID or a sibling: same prefix, different last digit.

Results

Clean: h's exact code ranked first in sibling rowsRQ-VAE 18 %, RQ-KMeans 53 %
… if h was re-bought by some user in trainingRQ-VAE 92 %, RQ-KMeans 96 %
RQ-VAE declared pooled estimate (P1)+0.09 nats [−0.02, +0.25] (test): includes 0

Takeaways

  • RQ-KMeans copies h's last digit. When the target is a sibling, this copy competes with it.
  • RQ-VAE does the opposite in sibling rows: blocking the edge makes it pick h's code more often and the sibling less often, so the read pushes it away from h. The declared pooled estimate for RQ-VAE includes 0; this rests on the top-1 changes.
  • The difference matches the maps: RQ-VAE's last digit mostly names one item, RQ-KMeans' last digit is shared by near-duplicates (structure exp3).

Source: derived/controlled/exp10_ar_last_digit_sibling/summary-293619-293620/

Controlled exp11

Copying across 12 retrained AR models

12 retrained Qwen-AR next-item models (MQ, RQ-KMeans, RQ-VAE; depth 3–5; width 128 and 512) · test and validation splits · declared protocol; run 2026-10-07, summarized 2026-10-15

What we did

We retrained the 18 AR next-item models of the width-128/512 grid with the recorded recipe (substrate exp1). Twelve passed the acceptance check against their archived lists; MQ 3×512, MQ 4×128, MQ 5×128, MQ 5×512, RQ-KMeans 3×512 and RQ-KMeans 4×512 did not. On each of the 12, we repeated four estimates from the two original models: replacing r1 (exp3), prefix-matched copying and the single-edge knockout (exp4), and blocking copying inside beam search on repeat targets (exp6). We also compared the retrained RQ-KMeans 3×128 with the original.

Results

Models whose interval excludes 0, all four estimates12 of 12
Replace r1, first digit0.37–0.78 nats
Prefix-matched copying (match − non-match)0.89–2.18 nats
Single-edge knockout (minus control edge)0.20–0.60 nats
Copy block in beam search, repeat targets−7.5 to −37.0 pp of HR@10
Retrained − original RQ-KMeans 3×128replace r1 −0.03 nats; copying −0.04 [−0.13, 0.05]; decoding −9.8 pp

Takeaways

  • Every retrained model copies, on every quantizer, depth and width tested. The copy findings are not specific to the two original checkpoints.
  • A second training run of the same map gives the same history-use numbers within 0.04 nats. The effect on repeat targets in decoding differs more (−37 vs −27 pp).
  • The six models that failed acceptance are not included.

Source: derived/controlled/exp11_ar_copy_grid/summary-301495/

Representation exp1

Layer-by-layer readout of the first digit

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · test split, activations at all 28 layers · declared protocol; observational

What we did

At the position that predicts the first digit, we applied the model's output head to every layer (logit lens). We also trained linear probes, with users split between training and test, for r1's first digit and the target's first digit.

Results

Final top-1 first digit = r1's first digitRQ-KMeans 64 % · RQ-VAE 53 %
Final top-1 first digit = the target's18 % · 34 %
Layer where the copy appears in the logit lens20–23 · 11 and 20
Probe for r1's first digit after block 084 % · 93 %
Probe for the target's first digit, any layernever above the rule 'predict r1's first digit'

Takeaways

  • The model's first digit is mostly a copy of the most recent item's first digit.
  • That digit is readable from the first layer, but the output starts to follow it only in late layers.
  • No layer holds information about the target beyond the copy rule.

Source: derived/representation/exp1_ar_digit_decoding/summary-281264-281411/

Representation exp2

Sparse autoencoders on the AR residual stream

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · SAEs trained on train-split activations, analysed on the test split · declared protocol; amendment A1 post hoc

What we did

We trained TopK sparse autoencoders (12,288 latents, k = 32) at layers 12, 16, 20 and 24. At the first-digit prediction position we looked for copy latents, which fire for one code of r1's first digit, and at later digits for match latents, which fire when r1 matches the prefix so far. We removed each set from the activation (keeping the SAE's error) and compared with matched control latents. Ridge and logistic probes tested for target content beyond the history.

Results

Removing copy latents: drop in the copy score0.10 nats at layer 20; 0.21 · 0.36 at layer 24
Share of the readout's latent activation they carry≤ 3 % · ≤ 12 %
Match latents: held-out AUC for 'r1 matches the prefix'up to 0.97 (RQ-KMeans), about 0.66 (RQ-VAE)
Removing match latents0.00 ± 0.04 nats (RQ-KMeans)
Readout predicts a same-day burst beyond SID overlapAUC +0.08–0.09

Takeaways

  • SAEs find copy features that change the output from layer 20 on.
  • Features that detect a prefix match exist at the prediction position but have no effect there. With exp4, this suggests the match is computed inside attention (query against key).
  • No target content beyond the history is readable.

Source: derived/representation/exp2_ar_sae/summary-287222-287231/

Representation exp3

Information map across all layers

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · test split, the model's own greedy answers · declared protocol; amendment A1

What we did

We let each model write its own greedy answer and captured every second layer. We trained SAEs at each of these layers and labelled every latent by what it tracks (a census). We also fitted a tuned lens and decoders that read the whole SID of the model's answer, the true target and r1 from each layer.

Results

Median first layer from which the answer stays readable: copy / other answers17 / 23 · 19 / 23
An item's last token holds its full SID fromlayer 2
True target decoded above 'output r1'at most +2.1 · +3.3 pp
Greedy answer = target10.9 % · 6.3 % of rows

Takeaways

  • Answers that copy the most recent item form earlier than other answers.
  • Each history item's identity is assembled in the first two layers.
  • As in representation exp1, no layer holds the true target beyond simple history rules.

Source: derived/representation/exp3_ar_information_map/summary-294711-294712/

Controlled exp6

Blocking copying inside beam search

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 · test split, archived decoder and plain beam search · declared protocol, two amendments

What we did

We re-ran the archived decoder and blocked the copy reads (exp4's edges, layers 14–27) at every digit, at later digits only, or, as a control, as many reads of non-matching items. Each beam is blocked from its own prefix. We measured HR@10 on repeat targets (SID already in the history) and new targets. The archived decoder samples (temperature 0.7, top-k 20, top-p 0.8, repetition penalty 1.1), because the checkpoint's generation settings were merged in; we reproduced it exactly and also ran plain beam search.

Results

Block at every digit: all targetsRQ-KMeans −5.7 · RQ-VAE −3.3 pp
… repeat targets (HR@10 91 % with copying)−27.3 · −10.1 pp
… new targets−2.1 · −3.0 pp
Control block−0.03 · −0.11 pp
Archived lists reproduced3,680 of 3,681

Takeaways

  • Copying helps the AR lists and never hurts them.
  • Most of the gain is on items the user already had. Retrospective exp7 shows that most of the gain on 'new' targets comes from items that share a SID with a history item or are near-duplicate variants.

Source: derived/controlled/exp6_ar_copy_in_decoding/summary-283114/

Retrospective exp7

Which targets the copy benefit comes from

exp6 predictions of RQ-KMeans 3×128 and RQ-VAE 4×128 · test split · declared protocol; amendment A1 post hoc

What we did

We re-scored exp6's lists at item level: each SID was expanded to every item it names. We split targets by how they relate to the history: the same item, a different item with the same SID (a collision partner), a near-duplicate variant with a different SID, or a truly new item.

Results

RQ-KMeans: share of the SID-level HR@1 copy benefit that remains at item level28 % [22, 36] (HR@10: 83 %)
RQ-VAE: share of exp6's 'copying helps new targets' carried by variants94 %

Takeaways

  • Copying recovers repeat purchases and product variants.
  • For RQ-KMeans, much of the benefit at rank 1 is credit for a SID that several items share; only 28 % of it remains at item level.

Retrospective exp3

Collisions and SID-level accuracy

18 archived AR next-item configurations · test split, saved lists · descriptive

What we did

We compared HR@10 for targets whose SID is shared by several items with targets whose SID is unique, within each configuration. We also expanded each predicted SID into its items and computed item-level HR@10 bounds.

Results

Configurations where collided targets are easier17 of 18
Pooled (not cell-averaged) collided − singleton+33.0 pp

RQ-KMeans 3×128, RQ-VAE 4×128 (and both DiffGRM matched models) · review days for every event · declared protocol

What we did

We recovered each event's review day and split the data, and the outputs of exp3, exp4, exp6 and exp7, by the gap between r1 and the target.

Targets on the same day as r141–50 %
RQ-KMeans copies r1's first digit: same day / more than a year67 % / 67 % (data: 33 % / 3 %)

What we did

We swapped r1 and r2 and measured how much the model prefers whichever item is last (position effect A) and how much it prefers the item that is truly later (item effect B). We split rows by whether the two items share a review day; when they do, only ASIN order separates them.

Under teacher forcing on 'item 1 ||| item 2', we replaced item 1 with a catalogue item, or replaced r1, and measured item 2's digits. We also tested prefix-matched copying from item 1 to item 2 and patched activations to find where item 1's information moves.

On this pageConfidence vs fixed reveal order in the archived runsConfidence vs fixed order at the same beam sizeAll six fixed orders at depth 3Reveal trace: what the decode holds at each stepWhat DiffGRM uses from the historyThe copy reaches the decoder through the encoderWhat the encoder holds: probes, SAEs and a description autoencoderActivation patching between paired runsAt which reveal step DiffGRM uses the historyPerturbations held through decoding: copy block, swap and shift
Provisional results. Every number on this page comes from the checkpoints we have now: two AR next-item models, one AR next-two model, 12 retrained AR models and 20 DiffGRM models. The paper's final numbers will come from rerunning the full analysis on the intermediate checkpoints of the final training run (with our co-author). We expect the trends to hold, but we have not checked that yet, so treat the values here as a preview of the write-up, not as its final results.

Diffusion experiments

DiffGRM is a masked-diffusion recommender. A one-layer encoder turns each history item (its SID digits, plus its slot position) into one state. A four-layer decoder has one position per SID digit; each position holds either a revealed code or a mask. Decoding starts with every digit masked, and at each step a beam search reveals one (position, code) pair; only the partial SID passes from one step to the next. We have 20 trained next-item models: MQ, RQ-KMeans and RQ-VAE at depths 3, 4 and 5 and widths 128 and 512, plus MQ 5×256 and RQ-VAE 3×256. Two of them, RQ-KMeans 3×128 and RQ-VAE 4×128, use the same SID maps as the two AR models. The test cohort is 6,297 users with their last item held out; it is a different cohort from the AR test split, so AR and DiffGRM numbers are compared side by side, never joined. In the width charts an open dot is width 128 and a filled dot width 512.

Representation exp5

What the encoder holds: probes, SAEs and a description autoencoder

20 DiffGRM models · 6,297 test users (36,783 slots); fitted on training-target histories · declared protocol, run 2026-10-14

What we did

We read the encoder at three points: its input, after self-attention, and its output. Linear probes tested what each slot holds about its own item, its recency, r1 and the target. TopK SAEs (2,048 latents, k = 16) on the output were labelled by what each latent tracks; we then removed the latents that carry r1's first code in the other slots (spread latents) and measured the copy score.

We also built a small version of a natural language autoencoder: a verbalizer writes each slot state as eight words (recency, category, store, price, first code, and what r1 looks like), and a reconstructor rebuilds the state from those words. We then measured how much decoder behaviour the rebuilt states keep, and which word the decoder needs most.

Results

RQ-KMeansRQ-VAEMQ
width 128 (filled)width 512 (open)
RQ-KMeansRQ-VAEMQwidth 128width 512
Own first code at the output (all models)0.31–0.53 (input 0.98–1.00)
Recency, output − input accuracy+0.20 to +0.31
Target's first code on new-target users, output − input−0.011 to +0.010
SAE: unexplained variance / behaviour kept by the splice0.06–0.25 / 0.87–0.99
Description: unexplained variance / behaviour kept0.44–0.76 / 0.39–0.85

Takeaways

  • The single encoder layer turns each slot from 'this item' into 'this user's recent context': a slot's own first code drops from almost perfectly readable to 31–53 %, while recency and r1's first code appear in every slot.
  • The encoder holds nothing about new targets beyond the history's content, the same as AR.
  • Spread latents change the output in 19 of 20 models; they are part of the route exp8 found.
  • Eight words keep 39–85 % of the decoder's behaviour, and the words it needs most describe the recent item.

Source: derived/representation/exp5_diffusion_encoder_features/summary-312763/

Controlled exp12

Activation patching between paired runs

20 DiffGRM models · 6,297 test users · declared protocol, run 2026-10-14 (on CPU)

What we did

We ran each model twice on inputs that differ in one thing. In part H, r1 is replaced (exp7's controls). In part S, the history is the same and one revealed digit holds a sibling's code. We copied pieces of one run into the other: encoder states of r1's slot or of the other slots, the decoder's state after each block at each digit position, and each block's cross-attention output. In part S we also cut the self-attention edge from the predicted digit to the changed digit.

Results

RQ-KMeansRQ-VAEMQwidth 128width 512
RQ-KMeansRQ-VAEMQ
width 128 (filled)width 512 (open)
RQ-KMeansRQ-VAEMQwidth 128width 512
Restored by other slots / r1's own slot (first digit)0.83–0.90 / 0.32–0.53
Noising: damage from the replaced history in other slots / r1's slot0.47–0.68 / 0.10–0.17
Edge share: depth 3 / depth 50.68–0.89 / 0.37–0.66

Takeaways

  • The replaced item reaches the decoder mostly through the other history slots, in every model.
  • Each digit position reads the history through its own cross-attention, spread over the four blocks; the best single block restores 0.34–0.77 of the effect, and the same patch at other digits at most 0.23.
  • A revealed digit's information reaches the digit being predicted in the first decoder block, mostly over the direct self-attention edge. The edge carries less at depth 5.

Users whose top-1 changes when r1 is replaced56–88 %
F(first step) / F(last step)0.16–0.68 / 0.01–0.10
F(first step), width 128 / 5120.16–0.39 / 0.25–0.68 (512 higher in 9 of 9 pairs)
Controlsno switch = plain decode and full switch = donor decode, bit for bit

Takeaways

  • The first reveal step decides most, but no single step decides alone: the history is used at every step.
  • Wider codebooks decide earlier: the first step matters more at width 512 than at 128 in all 9 pairs.
  • When one step changes the result, it usually changes which digit is revealed, not only its code.

Source: derived/controlled/exp13_diffusion_step_switch/summary-312774/

Controlled exp14

Perturbations held through decoding: copy block, swap and shift

19 DiffGRM models · 6,297 test users, beam 256 and 64 · declared protocol, run 2026-10-14/15

What we did

We held three changes for the whole beam search. First, we blocked every route to r1 (exp8's double block) and compared with the same block on an older item. Second, we swapped r1 and r2. Third, we moved the whole history one or five slots to the right, keeping the order.

Results

RQ-KMeansRQ-VAEMQwidth 128width 512
Copy block vs control, SID / item level−1.0 to −3.7 / −1.0 to −2.9 pp
Swap: users who copied r1 and switch to the item now last0–18 %
Shift by 5 slots: HR@10 change−0.5 to −3.5 pp
Models19 of 20 (MQ 5×512 failed the archive check)

Takeaways

  • Copying helps DiffGRM's lists, and only for items the user already had: −12 to −39 pp on repeat targets, about 0 on new targets. This is the AR pattern (AR exp6, retrospective exp7).
  • After a swap, DiffGRM keeps copying the same item even though it is no longer last; RQ-KMeans AR follows the position instead (AR exp9). The declared swap estimate was mis-scaled, so this rests on a post-hoc measure.
  • Moving the history changes the top-1 for 47–82 % of users: DiffGRM reads absolute slot positions. Training never put padding first, so part of this effect may come from that.

Source: derived/controlled/exp14_diffusion_decode_perturbations/summary-312775-313104/

On this pageWhat each SID digit encodesWhy items share a SID
Provisional results. Every number on this page comes from the checkpoints we have now: two AR next-item models, one AR next-two model, 12 retrained AR models and 20 DiffGRM models. The paper's final numbers will come from rerunning the full analysis on the intermediate checkpoints of the final training run (with our co-author). We expect the trends to hold, but we have not checked that yet, so treat the values here as a preview of the write-up, not as its final results.

SID maps (both models)

Both recommenders write semantic IDs from the same 27 maps: three quantizers (RQ-KMeans, RQ-VAE, MQ) × depth 3, 4 or 5 × codebook width 128, 256 or 512, over the 3,105 Industrial items. These two analyses look at the maps alone; no recommender is run. They come before the model experiments in the write-up because the model results depend on what a digit means in each map and on which items share a SID.

Structure exp1, exp2 and semantic mapping

What each SID digit encodes

27 SID maps · 3,105 items, item embeddings, Amazon category labels · descriptive, no model

What we did

For every map we measured how much of the item embedding and of the category one digit explains, alone and given the earlier digits; how many codes each digit uses; how large prefix groups are; how pure their categories are compared with a shuffled-label null; how much tighter they are than random groups of the same size; and how many items share a full SID.

Results

Embedding variance explained by digit 1 alone (4×128)RQ-KMeans 53 %, RQ-VAE 34 %, MQ 38 %
… by each later digit aloneRQ-KMeans 12–16 %, RQ-VAE 8–18 %, MQ 36–38 %
Category purity after 3 digits (null)RQ-KMeans 0.97 (0.45), RQ-VAE 0.99 (0.50), MQ 0.81 (0.39)
First-codebook codes used by RQ-VAE2–31 % in 8 of 9 fits
Items sharing a full SID, 3×128 (1 − unique/N)RQ-KMeans 29.3 %, RQ-VAE 1.2 %, MQ 40.1 %

Takeaways

  • In RQ-KMeans and RQ-VAE, digit 1 is a real partition of the catalogue and later digits refine it; a later digit means something only given the earlier digits.
  • MQ's digits are parallel partitions of similar quality that overlap; an MQ prefix is an intersection, not a step down a hierarchy.
  • The category is settled by digit 3; later digits separate items within a category.
  • RQ-VAE leaves most of its first codebook unused and makes its last digit an identity digit.

Source: derived/exp1_atlas/, derived/exp2_geometry/, derived/semantic_mapping/194268/; figures in docs/results/semantic_mapping/figures/

Structure exp3

Why items share a SID

27 SID maps, refits over 5 seeds · 3,105 items · declared protocol; amendments A1–A3 post hoc

What we did

We refitted the quantizers (reproducing the archived RQ-KMeans tables exactly), applied each map's post-processing to the others, and tested candidate causes of collisions: capacity, embedding norm, whitening, the shared k-means seed, a hub code, near-duplicate products, MQ's dependent digits, and RQ-VAE's last-digit reassignment.

Results

RQ-KMeans tables after the last-digit loopall at the identical-input floor: 22 items, 0.71 %
Collided items with a near-duplicate in their bucket (nested RQ-KMeans, deepest fits)73–85 %
Items in the hub code nearest the origin, each level ≥ 29–17 %
MQ: mean pairwise NMI between digits0.50–0.70

Takeaways

  • Each quantizer collides for a different reason. RQ-VAE's near-zero rate comes from a post-processing step that reassigns the last digit of colliding items; applied to RQ-KMeans, the same step removes nearly all of its collisions.
  • Near-duplicate products (same brand, nearly the same title) are the floor of collisions in every map.
  • MQ collides because its digits repeat each other. RQ-KMeans 5×512 is a separately balanced table, not the extension of the other RQ-KMeans tables.
  • Collision rates, and so SID-level hit rates, depend on post-processing as much as on the quantizer.

Source: derived/structure/exp3_collision_causes/293555/result/
